title: Ramayana Walks Into Hall H: Ranbir and Yash Eye a San Diego Comic-Con Trailer Drop Beside Marvel and Dune
excerpt: Nitesh Tiwari's ₹4,000-crore epic is being pitched to the world — a July Comic-Con launch, a TIFF march, and a rumoured Hans Zimmer–AR Rahman concert. The boldest flex Bollywood has tried in a decade.
body:
Picture it: Hall H at San Diego Comic-Con, the same cavernous room that has roared for *Avengers* and *Dune*, the lights drop — and instead of a caped American, the screen fills with a long-haired warrior holding a bow, a tilak on his brow, the score swelling into something that sounds like a temple bell crossed with a war drum. That is the gamble **Nitesh Tiwari** and producer **Namit Malhotra** are reportedly making this July, and if it lands, it will be the most audacious thing Indian cinema has ever tried on foreign soil.


The makers of **Ramayana** are in advanced talks to unveil the film's first full trailer at San Diego Comic-Con, running July 23–26, where it would share the marquee with *Avengers: Doomsday* and *Dune: Part Three*. Let that sink in. An adaptation of the *Ramayan* — the 7,000-year-old epic your grandmother recited from memory — pitched not as a regional curiosity but as a global tentpole, standing shoulder to shoulder with Marvel and Villeneuve.

> "The idea is to present the mythological drama not just as an Indian epic, but as a cinematic spectacle to the world."

That line, from the team's reported pitch, is the whole thesis. And they have the receipts to back the swagger. A focus-group screening in Los Angeles reportedly left a diverse, non-Indian audience genuinely moved — praising the scale, the grandeur, the emotional weight. An earlier IMAX showcase in LA, attended by **Ranbir Kapoor**, Tiwari, and Malhotra, did the same. CinemaCon got a taste. The confidence is no longer just Mumbai bravado; it's been stress-tested in front of the toughest, most franchise-fatigued crowd on earth.

Then there's the cast, and frankly, it reads like a fantasy XI. **Ranbir Kapoor** as Lord Rama — leaner, longer-haired, serene yet coiled, in a teaser that pulled 18 million views in its first 24 hours. **Yash**, the *KGF* juggernaut, as Ravana, his first look reportedly being held back as a Comic-Con grenade. **Sai Pallavi** as Sita, which might be the most quietly perfect casting of the lot — there is no actress working today who radiates that particular warmth. **Sunny Deol** as Hanuman. **Ravie Dubey** as Lakshman. And circling the project: Arun Govil (yes, *that* Ram, the one a generation grew up worshipping on Doordarshan), Lara Dutta, Vivek Oberoi, Kajal Aggarwal, Rakul Preet Singh, with Amitabh Bachchan and Bobby Deol reportedly in talks.

The budget is the part that makes Hollywood executives spit out their coffee: a reported ₹4,000-crore-plus ($400–500 million) across two parts, making it comfortably the most expensive Indian film ever mounted. That number has invited scrutiny — leaked set photos of Ranbir's wig drew a brutal Reddit roasting ("All that $400 million budget and they couldn't arrange for a decent-looking wig?"). The makers stayed silent, which is its own kind of confidence.

But the masterstroke isn't the trailer. It's October. The team is reportedly planning a live concert built around a *historic* collaboration between two Oscar winners — **Hans Zimmer** and **AR Rahman** — performing the film's score together. Zimmer's thunder and Rahman's soul, scoring the Ramayan, live. If that happens, it transcends film promotion entirely and becomes a cultural event.

**For the diaspora, this is the headline.** A San Diego Comic-Con launch means NRIs in California don't have to wait for a Mumbai feed at 4 a.m. — the trailer drops in *their* timezone, on *their* turf, at the convention many of them already attend in cosplay. There are even whispers the trailer could be attached to US theatrical screenings of *The Odyssey*, and that the film will tour Toronto, London BFI, and Tokyo festivals before release. After Comic-Con, the road reportedly runs through TIFF — a deliberate march through the West's prestige circuit.

Part One is set for **Diwali 2026**, with Part Two following in 2027. The symbolism writes itself: Rama returning home, on the festival of his return, on screens from Edison to Southall to Brampton.

Here's the honest take. This could be a generational triumph — the film that finally makes the world watch an Indian epic on its own terms — or it could be a $500-million swing that misses, undone by VFX that can't cash the cheques the ambition wrote. The teaser was promising; the wig discourse was not. But you cannot fault the nerve. Walking the Ramayan into Hall H is the boldest flex Bollywood has attempted in a decade. Come July 23, we find out if the bow can bend.
